articles.body: Services Sticky News ESL expands Far East-Africa network with FAX2 and FAX3 services November 2, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Photo: Emirates Shipping Line Emirates Shipping Line (ESL) will launch two new services connecting major Chinese ports with East and southeastern Africa. The new Far East Africa Express 2 (FAX2) and Far East Africa Express 3 (FAX3) services will complement ESL’s existing Far East Africa Express network. The FAX2 service will connect Qingdao, Ningbo and Nansha with Mombasa through Port Klang. Its first sailing is scheduled to depart Qingdao on 5 December 2026. The FAX2 rotation will be: Qingdao – Ningbo – Nansha – Port Klang – Mombasa – Qingdao FAX3 will provide a direct connection to Maputo, Mozambique. According to ESL, the service will also support access to neighbouring markets, including Eswatini, Zimbabwe and South Africa. The first FAX3 sailing is scheduled to depart Shanghai on 25 November 2026. The FAX3 rotation will be: Shanghai – Ningbo – Nansha – Port Klang – Dar es Salaam – Maputo – Singapore – Shanghai The two services will operate alongside ESL’s existing FAX service, which connects Qingdao, Shanghai, Ningbo, Nansha and Port Klang with Dar es Salaam and Mombasa. articles.title: SCHOTTEL Unveils New Thruster for Submarines and Underwater Vehicles
articles.summary: German propulsion specialist SCHOTTEL has introduced a new submersible auxiliary thruster designed to improve maneuverability and positioning accuracy for crewed and uncrewed underwater vehicles, including submarines.The SCHOTTEL PumpJet Submersible…
articles.body: SCHOTTEL Unveils New Thruster for Submarines and Underwater Vehicles Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 SCHOTTEL PumpJet Submersible SPJ-S (Credit: SCHOTTEL) German propulsion specialist SCHOTTEL has introduced a new submersible auxiliary thruster designed to improve maneuverability and positioning accuracy for crewed and uncrewed underwater vehicles, including submarines. The SCHOTTEL PumpJet Submersible SPJ-S provides continuously adjustable thrust through 360 degrees and is designed for civil and military underwater operations, including deepwater missions and maneuvering in confined spaces. The electrically driven system uses an impeller without a gearbox, enabling low-noise operation, while a pressure compensation system equalizes hydrostatic pressure at the seals to support operations at greater depths. Unlike retractable auxiliary propulsion systems, the SPJ-S provides immediate thrust without requiring deployment before use. The thruster is installed flush with the hull to avoid additional hydrodynamic resistance and reduce the risk of damage from seabed contact. Its construction also enables controlled bottoming on the seabed. The compact system can be integrated into platforms ranging from extra-large unmanned underwater vehicles (XLUUVs) to submarines. In addition to providing auxiliary propulsion, the SPJ-S can serve as a take-home propulsion system to maintain maneuverability in the event of main propulsion failure. The thruster is available in three sizes, covering a power range of approximately 50 to 990 kW. SCHOTTEL will present the SPJ-S for the first time at Euronaval 2026, taking place in Paris from November 3 to 6.

REUTERS/Jean-Paul Pelissier/File Photo By Rob Verdonck and Nicholas Lua Nov 2, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Goldman Sachs Group Inc. raised oil-price forecasts for the year-end and 2027 on elevated risks to supplies, joining other banks in hiking their outlooks after months of war in the Middle East. Brent is now seen at $105 a barrel in December, up from a previous estimate of $90, and will average $88 next year, 10% more than seen before, analysts including Daan Struyven and Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby said in a note, which also increased forecasts for US oil marker West Texas Intermediate. “Substantial downside supply risks are likely to sustain a large, near-term risk premium,” the analysts wrote. The markets are assigning “increasing weight to escalation after the Nov. 3 US midterms and subsequent potential weakness in Mideast supply,” they added in the Nov. 1 report. Global benchmark Brent rallied 14% in October, hitting a six-month high, even as crude supplies from the Middle East rebounded close to pre-war levels. The gains came on concern that hostilities between the US and Iran may flare up again after the midterm elections, with President Donald Trump repeatedly hinting that he may resume airstrikes. For his part, Iran’s supreme leader has ordered his top commanders to prepare for renewed confrontation. Intensified shipping attacks and damage to infrastructure were among factors that could trigger further price gains, the analysts said, while also highlighting risks from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “With the timing and location of disruptions nearly impossible to predict, our base case now includes a 1-million-barrel-per-day global supply disruption allowance in 2027.” Beyond its core view, Goldman also sketched bullish and bearish frameworks for 2027 with prices spanning a range of about $70, highlighting the challenges facing forecasters as they grapple with a wide range of potential outcomes. In the bank’s upside scenario, Brent may average $130 next year if Persian Gulf output remains 3.5 million barrels a day below last year’s average, the analysts said. But in the downside version, marked by a faster recovery in regional output, futures “might decline into the $60s,” they said. In recent weeks, Morgan Stanley raised its forecast for Dated Brent — a key physical price — to $105 a barrel for the fourth quarter, while ANZ Group Holdings Ltd. hiked its year-end outlook for Brent futures to the same figure. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky ABU DHABI, Nov 2 (Reuters) – The UAE will protect its energy infrastructure and invest in new export routes, storage capacity abroad and shipping fleets to be better prepared for the US-Israeli war on Iran, its energy minister said on Monday. Minister Suhail al-Mazrouei said the course of the war could not be predicted, but the UAE would be more prepared than before. The UAE has been exporting crude via Fujairah, which sits just outside the Strait of Hormuz. It is building a new pipeline to Fujairah that will double crude capacity by next year. “I think after this crisis, many companies are going to look, think again, and design, redesign their facilities to be more resilient in the future,” Mazrouei told reporters on the sidelines of the Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition and Conference. “Resilience is a big word. And it has layers, from the barrel that you produce to the destination that you take it,” he said, adding: “You need to be closer to your customers.” Mazrouei earlier told the conference that at certain times his country’s exports were higher than prior to the war. Reuters had reported in June that the UAE boosted crude oil and condensate exports to a record high , shortly after it left the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Plaquemines LNG Courtesy of Venture Global U.S. liquefied natural gas (LNG) export project developer Venture Global has reached commercial operations (COD) for the first phase of its Plaquemines LNG export facility in Louisiana, hitting the milestone just over 53 months after making its final investment decision (FID), a project described as one of the fastest greenfield LNG developments ever completed. articles.body: Europe Offshore OMV Petrom chief to exit as Neptun Deep nears first gas Bojan Lepic November 2, 2026 0 0 1 minute read OMV Petrom OMV Petrom Romanian oil and gas producer OMV Petrom is preparing for a leadership change as chief executive Christina Verchere has announced she will not seek another term, with her departure set to occur around the planned startup of the company’s flagship Neptun Deep gas development in the Black Sea. Verchere, who has led the company since May 2018, told supervisory board chair Emma Delaney she will not be available for another mandate after her current term expires on April 16, 2027. The company has not named a successor or disclosed the reasons behind her decision. “It has been a privilege for me to lead OMV Petrom for these past 9 years,” Verchere said, adding that she remained committed to delivering the company’s strategic projects during her remaining time in office. Her departure comes as OMV Petrom moves towards first gas from the €4bn ($4.48bn) Neptun Deep development, one of the largest offshore energy projects in the Black Sea. The company and its 50:50 partner Romgaz expect production to begin in the first half of 2027, with plateau output of around 8bn cubic metres annually targeted by the end of the third quarter. The development, located around 160 km offshore Romania, holds estimated recoverable resources of approximately 100bn cubic metres of gas. OMV Petrom’s latest quarterly update showed that eight of the ten planned development wells were completed, along with the installation of the Neptun Alpha production platform and the gas export pipeline to shore. The project was sanctioned in 2023 during Verchere’s tenure and is expected to transform Romania into a major regional gas supplier. Before joining OMV Petrom, Verchere spent more than two decades at BP, holding senior positions including regional president for Canada and Asia Pacific. articles.body: Nakilat Names Nine New Gas Carriers in South Korea Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 (Credit Nakilat) Qatar Gas Transport Company (Nakilat) has named nine new gas carriers at three South Korean shipyards, marking progress in its fleet expansion programs aimed at increasing LNG transportation capacity and diversifying into LPG/ammonia shipping. The naming ceremonies, announced on November 2, took place at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, Hanwha Ocean and HD Hyundai Samho, covering seven LNG carriers and two LPG/ammonia carriers. Five of the LNG carriers form part of Nakilat's 25-vessel conventional-size LNG carrier newbuild program at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean. The 25 vessels will be fully owned and operated by Nakilat and chartered to QatarEnergy affiliates under long-term agreements, supporting LNG transportation requirements associated with Qatar's North Field expansion projects. The other four vessels, comprising two LNG carriers and two LPG/ammonia carriers, belong to Nakilat's separate six-vessel newbuild program at HD Hyundai Samho. The seven LNG carriers were named Al Ghuwair, Al Jazi, Al Mirzam, Maqdeem, Al Nasraniya, Energy Vigour and Energy Voyager, while the two LPG/ammonia carriers were named Energy South and Energy East. “We are proud of our partnership with QatarEnergy, through which we aim to deliver added value to the LNG transportation market as an active partner in meeting the requirements of the North Field expansion projects. “The naming of these nine vessels represents tangible progress in Nakilat’s long-term investment in expanding its fleet. By strengthening our LNG transportation capabilities and further diversifying our fleet with LPG/ammonia carriers, we are enhancing our ability to respond to our customers’ evolving needs while continuing to support Qatar’s position as one of the world’s leading producers and exporters of LNG,” said Abdullah Al Sulaiti, Chief Executive Officer of Nakilat The LNG newbuilds will support gas transportation from Qatar to international markets, while the LPG/ammonia carriers will expand Nakilat's range of shipping services. articles.title: PortXchange Expands Emissions Platform with Forecasting, AI Tools
articles.summary: Dutch maritime technology company PortXchange is expanding its EmissionInsider platform with emissions forecasting, scenario modelling and AI-assisted decarbonization planning tools to help ports assess the environmental impact of their operations…
articles.body: PortXchange Expands Emissions Platform with Forecasting, AI Tools Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 Sjoerd De Jager, Managing Director of PortXchange (Credit: PortXchange) Dutch maritime technology company PortXchange is expanding its EmissionInsider platform with emissions forecasting, scenario modelling and AI-assisted decarbonization planning tools to help ports assess the environmental impact of their operations and future investments. The planned upgrade will also introduce multimodal emissions monitoring, bringing together emissions data from vessels, trucks, rail movements and cargo-handling equipment, the company said. The expanded platform will comprise four connected products: Emission Report, Emission Dashboard, Emission Simulations and Emission Strategy. Emission Report will provide structured reporting for ports with different levels of data availability, while Emission Dashboard will support regular monitoring of port activity and emissions performance. The forecasting capabilities are being developed to help ports anticipate short-term emissions changes caused by factors such as weather disruptions, vessel schedule changes and increased waiting times at berths or anchorages. Emission Simulations will allow ports to assess the potential impact of investments and operational changes, including shore power installation, port equipment electrification, vessel speed limits and increased traffic volumes. The Emission Strategy product will introduce AI-assisted support for developing and reviewing decarbonisation plans, helping ports identify measures and priorities based on their operations, emissions profiles and objectives. “Ports have become much better at measuring emissions, but measuring them doesn’t make them disappear. “If the information sits in a report that nobody uses when making operational or investment decisions, we have to question what we’re achieving. Ports need to know where they can make a difference, what it will cost and whether their plans will actually reduce emissions,” said Sjoerd de Jager, Managing Director and Co-Founder of PortXchange. PortXchange plans to introduce the new capabilities progressively, with a modular structure allowing ports to select products and data integrations according to their operational and decarbonisation requirements.

articles.body: Exploration & Production November 2, 2026 · 1 minute ago Gas flows from Southeast Asian offshore field 21 months after FID Eni and Petronas’ Searah has brought online an Asian gas field, flowing 250 million standard cubic feet per day (scfd) to domestic and export markets. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email FPU Jangkrik Source: Eni Searah, a joint venture (JV) between Italy’s Eni and Malaysia’s Petronas, has achieved first gas from the Maha gas field in the Kutei Basin just 21 months after its final investment decision (FID), boosting regional energy security and liquefied natural gas (LNG) capacity. Eni has announced the start-up of gas production from the Maha field in the West Ganal block at Indonesia’s Kutei Basin at a water depth of approximately 1,000 meters. This field comprises two subsea production wells connected to the existing Jangkrik floating production unit (FPU) by approximately 12 kilometers of flowlines. Following initial processing onboard the FPU, the gas will be transported through the pipeline network to supply the domestic market and the Bontang liquefaction plant, which supplies LNG to both domestic and export markets. The Maha field can produce 250 million standard cubic feet per day, bringing combined production from the Jangkrik FPU and the South Hub to a plateau of 750 million scfd. The Gendalo and Gendang project’s expected start-up and tie-in to the same FPU in 2028 will extend this plateau beyond the end of the decade. According to Eni, the execution and start-up of production at Maha, following the start-up of Merakes East in May 2025, together with the final investment decisions announced in March 2026 for the North Hub ( Geng North and Gehem ) and South Hub (Gendalo and Gendang) projects, underscore its broader strategy to efficiently develop the gas resources discovered in Indonesia’s Kutei Basin. articles.body: DNV’s Insight: 53 New Orders for Alternative-Fueled Vessels in October Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 (Credit: DNV) October maintained the strong pace of contracting for alternative-fueled vessels observed since the summer, with 53 new orders recorded during the month, according to DNV’s Alternative Fuels Insight (AFI) platform. LNG accounted for 30 of October’s orders. Container ships remained at the forefront of these, with 18 vessels ordered, while car carriers contributed a further 12. The month also saw 19 orders for LPG carriers, adding to continued activity across the alternative-fuelled fleet. In addition, four ammonia-fuelled car carriers were added to the database, representing another step towards building experience with ammonia as a marine fuel and supporting the gradual maturation of the technology. The latest figures bring the total number of alternative-fuelled vessels ordered in 2026 to 364, 57% higher than over the same period in 2025. LNG continues to dominate newbuild activity in the alternative-fuelled space, accounting for 230 orders so far this year. Container ships represent the largest share of these, with 134 vessels (58%), followed by 75 car carriers (32%). “October’s figures add to the strong activity we have seen in alternative-fuelled vessel ordering since the summer. Particularly notable is the continued concentration of LNG-fuelled orders in container ships and car carriers. “Together, these segments account for almost nine in ten LNG-fuelled orders placed this year, underlining the important role of shipping segments with close links to consumer supply chains in driving uptake. “LNG’s continued prominence is also supported by the comparatively mature infrastructure and supply chain around the fuel. A growing bunker vessel fleet and established fuel supply provide practical advantages over some other alternative fuels, while the potential to transition towards lower-carbon alternatives offers shipowners valuable optionality over the lifetime of their vessels,” said Jason Stefanatos, Global Decarbonization Director at DNV Maritime.

articles.summary: Fairbanks Morse Defense (FMD) has unveiled AutoHook, an autonomous vessel recovery interface developed by its Norway-based business Vestdavit, designed to recover uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) and other craft without manual connections.Introduced at EURONAVAL 2026 in Paris on November 2…
articles.body: Fairbanks Morse Defense Unveils Autonomous Vessel Recovery System Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 Illustration (Credit: Fairbanks Morse Defense - FMD) Fairbanks Morse Defense (FMD) has unveiled AutoHook, an autonomous vessel recovery interface developed by its Norway-based business Vestdavit, designed to recover uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) and other craft without manual connections. Introduced at EURONAVAL 2026 in Paris on November 2, the system is designed to automate the active recovery phase of launch and recovery operations, with FMD reporting that it has achieved operational acceptance at Sea State 4. AutoHook uses onboard vision technology and integrated thrusters to track and secure moving vessels during recovery, eliminating the need for crew intervention during the capture process. Following deployment of a mechanical floating catching device, the system autonomously tracks, secures and recovers the vessel. The compact unit clamps onto an existing davit wire and integrates its thrusters, control systems, vision technology and power supply into a single assembly, without requiring modifications to winches or davits. FMD said the technology is designed for interoperability across allied naval fleets and supports operations involving both crewed and uncrewed assets. FMD: Solving the Navy’s Tough Problems “The global shift toward distributed maritime operations depends on unmanned systems that perform in real-world conditions and integrate seamlessly across allied fleets. AutoHook not only supports fleet modernisation, it breaks the Sea State 2 ceiling that has long constrained manual launch and recovery,” said Rolf Andreas Wigand, FMD Managing Director of Davits. The system is intended to reduce crew exposure during vessel recovery in demanding maritime conditions, while allowing integration with existing shipboard equipment.

Orders increased 126% from $150 million (€135 million) in the same quarter last year, lifting the company's order book to $1.49 billion (€1.34 billion) at the end of September, compared with $1.11 billion (€998.6 million) a year earlier. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump had not decided whether to launch fresh strikes and that a diplomatic settlement remained possible. Tehran’s demands include sanctions relief, the release of frozen funds, restored oil waivers, and recognition of a shipping route designated with Oman. Iran also wants a reduced U.S. military presence and an end to attacks on Lebanon. Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei said a letter from Vice President JD Vance signaled a more conciliatory U.S. tone, but insisted Tehran would not reopen Hormuz before its conditions were met. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered commanders to prepare an immediate response to any attack without geographical restrictions, and Iranian officials threatened strikes against a wider range of targets. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said two oil tankers exploded after striking mines while travelling through an “unauthorized route” in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported on Sunday. Iran has imposed restrictions on vessels seeking to transit the waterway and attacked ships it says have violated those restrictions, as Tehran seeks to assert control over the strategic passage and increase pressure on Washington. U.S. Central Command said its blockade of Iranian ports had redirected 144 commercial ships, underscoring the growing disruption to maritime traffic through the region. Disruption to the waterway continues to threaten global energy supplies. articles.body: Vale freight, fuel hedges cushion impact of rising shipping costs in International Shipping News 02/11/2026 Brazilian miner Vale SA’s freight and fuel hedging strategies have protected the company from the worst impacts of higher shipping costs facing iron ore producers, CEO Gustavo Pimenta said. About 75% of Vale’s shipping needs are covered by long-term contracts at fixed prices over the next few years, while the remaining needs will be managed through shorter-term contracts. “This structure provides flexibility while limiting direct exposure to the spot market,” Pimenta said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call. The war in the Middle East has ratcheted up global fuel prices, contributing to higher maritime freight costs for Brazilian iron ore producers. Several producers have halted or reduced production because of the high rates. Vale’s realized freight costs increased by $4.70/metric ton since the first quarter, much less than the spot cost from Brazil to China, according to Pimenta. Over the same period, spot freight rates for the Brazil-China route increased by $12/mt, compared with $4.90/mt for the route from Australia to China, Pimenta said. The company’s all-in cost for the third quarter was $60.40/mt, up 21% year on year due to a stronger Brazilian real and higher diesel and bunker fuel prices. Vale’s all-in cost including the cash benefit from its oil hedging program was $59/mt, according to Marcelo Bacci, executive vice president for finance and investor relations. Vale has hedged 67% of its expected 2027 bunker consumption, at an average hedge price equivalent to $78/barrel Brent. The company’s freight strategy is expected to generate a benefit of more than $3 billion versus spot freight in 2026. “Our freight and hedging strategies provide meaningful protection in a more volatile market environment, helping preserve competitiveness and free cash flow generation,” Pimenta said. The company estimates its 2027 freight guidance exposure at $24-$25/mt based on current market prices. However, Vale is not yet locking in guidance levels because it expects better marker opportunities. C1 cash costs in the third quarter were $23.1/mt, 12% higher than the same time last year, largely due to higher diesel costs and appreciation of the Brazilian real. articles.title: The cost of almost: what trade at its full potential really means

articles.body: The cost of almost: what trade at its full potential really means in International Shipping News 02/11/2026 At any given moment, thousands of vessels are at sea. Each voyage is shaped by a series of decisions: speed, route, fuel, vessel performance, timing and execution. There is rarely one obviously right choice. A slower vessel may burn less fuel but arrive too late to capture the value of the cargo. A faster voyage may cost more in bunkers but create a better commercial outcome. A route that looked optimal at departure may no longer be the best option as weather, markets or port conditions develop. Shipping has always operated in these trade-offs. Minimising fuel, maximising speed or optimising any one variable is only part of the equation. The bigger challenge is understanding the commercial, operational and environmental consequences together – and making the best possible decision for that voyage, at that moment. Across one decision, the difference may be marginal. Across thousands of decisions, hundreds of vessels and an entire year, it can become material. That is the cost of almost. Every voyage contains unrealised possibilities There is the voyage that happened. There are also alternative ways that the same voyage could have been executed – different combinations of speed, route, fuel, timing and operational choices that may have produced a stronger result under the conditions and constraints at the time. Not every difference is avoidable or commercially relevant. And hindsight is easy. What matters is the avoidable part of the gap: fuel burned without creating additional value, time lost in unnecessary waiting, effort spent coordinating information across disconnected workflows, or opportunities that are harder to act on than they need to be. Shipping is a continuous balancing act between commercial priorities, contractual obligations, operational realities and changing conditions. Different companies in the value chain also carry different costs, risks and incentives. None of that complexity can be easily removed. But unnecessary waste within it can be reduced. Sustainable is a commercial word This is also why sustainability should not be treated as an environmental outcome alone. A trading system that is environmentally responsible but not commercially viable is not sustainable. Nor is one that performs efficiently in stable conditions but cannot absorb disruption. Sustainability, in its fuller sense, is about the ability to keep performing over time. In shipping, those dimensions are closely connected. The same operational decisions shape cost, voyage economics, resilience and emissions. Trade operating at its full potential therefore means balancing them well: commercially precise, operationally resilient and environmentally responsible as the natural outcome of better operations. Commercially precise. Decisions on speed, route, fuel and vessel performance made with a clear understanding of their commercial consequences. Operationally resilient. The ability to keep performing through disruption, uncertainty and changing conditions without losing sight of the wider voyage objective. Environmentally responsible. An outcome shaped by the same decisions that determine commercial and operational performance. That is what full potential looks like: better use of the information, assets and choices now available – and less avoidable waste in how the system operates. The constraint is structural Masters, operators, performance analysts and bunker traders make complex decisions every day, often under time pressure and across multiple commercial and operational priorities. The challenge can be applying that expertise consistently across large-scale operations. Voyage, vessel, bunker, weather and port information often sit across different systems and workflows. Turning that information into coordinated action can still require multiple people, systems and hand-offs. At scale, that matters. Time-sensitive opportunities can be missed because acting on them consistently still takes considerable manual effort. That is where the next opportunity for maritime technology sits. From insight to action For years, maritime technology has helped operators organise data, generate insight and make more informed decisions. That has created real value. Better forecasting, routing, vessel performance analysis and bunker planning have improved the quality of decision-making across the industry. But there is still a gap between seeing what should happen and making it happen consistently across the operation. That is where the current wave of AI becomes interesting. The significance of agentic AI is not that it suddenly understands shipping better than the people running it. It is that it can increasingly take on defined parts of the coordination work around those people. Within clear boundaries, systems will be able to work across data sources, carry out routine operational steps and bring people in when judgement, authority or experience is required. That matters because much of the remaining opportunity in shipping sits in the distance between insight and execution. The more effectively that distance can be closed, the more consistently operators can act on the opportunities already visible to them. This does not remove complexity. Nor should it. The value lies in helping maritime experts manage that complexity with greater precision and at greater scale, while keeping operators and masters firmly in control. Engineered, not assumed Sustainable trade will not be created through ambition alone. It will be engineered through better decisions, better coordination and better use of the data, technology and expertise already available across the industry. Progress will come from understanding the complexity of the system, working within the constraints and improving how the parts work together. One better decision rarely transforms a fleet. Thousands of better-informed decisions, made and acted on more consistently, can. That is what it means to engineer sustainable trade. More than green At ZeroNorth, this is the thinking behind our new vision. Since ZeroNorth was founded, more than 13,400 vessels have operated on our platform, giving us access to vessel and voyage data equivalent to ⅓ of the global merchant fleet. Today, we work with more than 200 customers and draw on a data foundation of 1.3 trillion data points annually. 50 million metric tonnes of bunker fuel have been transacted on our platform. That scale, combined with deep maritime expertise, has taught us a great deal about what it takes to turn data into better operational decisions. It has also reinforced something more fundamental: commercial performance, operational resilience and environmental responsibility cannot be treated as separate questions. Through our work across voyage, vessel and fuel, and through the development of Propel, we are building towards a model where technology can do more than surface insight. It can help coordinate defined operational work, connect decisions across domains and support maritime experts in acting on opportunities more consistently. Our ambition is to help the industry handle its complexity better – and remove more of the waste so that global trade can thrive. That, to us, is what sustainable trade means: trade operating closer to its full potential – commercially precise, operationally resilient and environmentally responsible as the natural outcome. articles.body: Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have announced plans to reroute their Gemini Cooperation Indian Ocean Service (IOS) through the Red Sea and Suez Canal, replacing the longer route around the Cape of Good Hope. The decision follows a review of the security situation in the region. According to the carriers, the revised routing will provide more efficient connections between India and Europe. The changes are scheduled to take effect in November 2026, with the first sailings already identified. Gemini ME1/IOS service returns to Suez Canal route Hapag-Lloyd refers to the service as IOS, while Maersk identifies it as ME1. Both carriers have confirmed the transition to the trans-Suez corridor. According to Maersk, the revised service will follow the rotation: Mundra – Nhava Sheva – Salalah – Suez Canal – Tangier – Rotterdam – Wilhelmshaven – Hamburg – London – Algeciras – Tangier – Suez Canal – Salalah – Mundra. The first scheduled westbound sailing will involve Atlanta Express , voyage 644W, departing Salalah on 4 November 2026. Meanwhile, Savannah Express , voyage 644E, will operate the first eastbound sailing under the revised arrangement. Hapag-Lloyd lists 12 November as the vessel’s estimated departure date from Tangier, while Maersk indicates 13 November. Both dates remain subject to operational conditions. The revised routing will allow the service to avoid the longer diversion around the Cape of Good Hope. As a result, the carriers expect more efficient transit times for cargo moving between India and Europe. The move represents another operational adjustment within the Gemini Cooperation network as Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd gradually reassess the use of the Red Sea corridor. However, the announcement concerns the ME1/IOS service specifically and does not indicate that the entire Gemini network is returning to the Suez Canal. Both carriers stated that they will continue monitoring security developments in the region. Any further routing adjustments will depend on prevailing conditions, with crew safety, vessel security and cargo protection remaining priorities.

articles.title: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
articles.summary: China and Russia are tightening their grip on Arctic shipping routes, turning the rapidly warming region into a new geopolitical battleground with Europe. articles.body: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back? in International Shipping News 02/11/2026 China and Russia are tightening their grip on Arctic shipping routes, turning the rapidly warming region into a new geopolitical battleground with Europe. Moscow and Beijing last week have agreed to expand freight traffic along Arctic shipping corridors, increase services between their ports and deepen cooperation on building polar vessels. The agreement came after the EU unveiled a new Arctic strategy aimed at countering growing Russian and Chinese influence in the region. Although the competing moves underscore how the once-remote region is turning into a strategic prize, analysts said that Europe’s ability to challenge the emerging China-Russia partnership remains limited, given Moscow’s control over the main shipping corridor and Beijing’s growing commercial clout. ‘’Europe cannot realistically challenge Chinese and Russian dominance of Arctic shipping in any meaningful timeframe.’’ Alicia Garcia-Herrero, APAC & MEA Chief Economist, Natixis CIB That’s because Moscow controls the Northern Sea Route, including shipping permits, transit fees and a vast fleet of nuclear icebreakers, while Beijing provides the cargo, vessels and industrial capacity needed to develop the corridor, she added. Europe, by contrast, has limited icebreaker capacity and Arctic infrastructure, leaving it with little leverage to challenge the partnership despite its position as a major destination market. A new geopolitical fault line? The Northern Sea Route offers itself as an increasingly attractive alternative, as Middle East disruptions expose vulnerabilities in established shipping corridors. Cargo traveling between Asia and Europe through the Northern Sea Route could have its journey shortened to between 18 to 22 days, down approximately 35% from the 28 to 35 day journey through Suez, according to data provided by Fertmax FZCO. For Moscow, the route offers an opportunity to redirect energy exports toward Asia as Western sanctions constrain its access to European markets, said industry watchers whom CNBC spoke to. On the other hand, it provides Beijing another trade artery that could reduce reliance on traditional maritime chokepoints. David Roche, a veteran strategist at Quantum Strategy & Geonomics, said the Arctic’s importance lies less in its potential to transform global shipping than in the deepening economic dependence between Russia and China. “The significance of the arctic route is for Russian energy shipments to China, which will increase China’s control over Russia in terms of Russia’s dependence on China to sell its energy to compensate for losses of its gas markets in Europe,” Roche highlighted. The EU has acknowledged the growing challenge, highlighting the region’s strategic value in its strategy, as mentioned by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas last week. ‘’With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition.’’ Kaja Kallas Foreign Policy Chief, European Union Can Europe fight back? Europe isn’t entirely without leverage. The EU’s new strategy calls for expanding European icebreaker capacity, strengthening maritime surveillance and developing infrastructure linking Arctic trade networks to European markets. It also proposes a maritime security hub and greater protection for undersea cables, reflecting growing concerns about Russian military activity and threats to critical infrastructure. Yet those strengths may not be enough to overturn the structural advantages enjoyed by Moscow and Beijing, said experts. Garcia-Herrero said Europe’s leverage largely rests on its position as a major destination market and the presence of large shipping companies that have avoided the Arctic because of environmental and commercial risks. ‘’Without a sustained industrial push that the EU has only begun to discuss, Europe can raise the commercial and regulatory costs of the route, but cannot prevent or replace the China-Russia partnership that now operates it.’’ Alicia Garcia-Herrero APAC & MEA Chief Economist, Natixis CIB Europe also faces a strategic dilemma: engaging with the emerging corridor could deepen its reliance on Russian-controlled infrastructure, even as it seeks to reduce Moscow’s economic influence. Fertmax FZCO’s former global head of research, Daeijin Lee said Western operators face sanctions, insurance and compliance complications that make the route considerably less attractive than it is for Chinese companies. “The Arctic gives diversification, not independence,” he said. A threat to global trade? For all the geopolitical attention, the Arctic remains a marginal player in global shipping. Roche estimates Arctic trade accounts for roughly 0.3% of global shipping today and could reach about 1% by 2030. Data from Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom and CNBC calculations based on UN Trade and Development figures similarly supports the 0.3% figure, with 37.02 million tonnes of cargo transiting the Northern Sea Route in 2025 compared to the 12.72 billion tonnes of global seaborne trade in 2024. Only 3.2 million tonnes of that cargo, or less than a tenth, involved vessels transiting the entire route, rather than shipments originating or terminating in the Russian Arctic, according to the Centre for High North Logistics. But traffic may be picking up, the latest September 2026 CHNL data showed. The route recorded 104 confirmed transit voyages carrying an estimated 3.7 million tonnes of cargo by the end of September, exceeding the 3.2 million tonnes recorded during the entire 2025 navigation season. Much of the existing traffic consists of Russian oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities rather than international container shipments. However, the route also faces significant commercial hurdles. Ice conditions restrict navigation for much of the year, while specialized vessels, insurance premiums and Russian transit fees can erode savings from shorter voyages. Matthew Wright, an analyst at Kpler, said the route remains poorly suited to replacing established shipping corridors because operators need reliable, year-round services. Lee similarly expects the Arctic to develop primarily as a seasonal express route for selected high-value cargo rather than a replacement for Suez. However, climate change could shift the balance in the long-term. A study published in the WMU Journal of Maritime Affairs projected that melting Polar ice could increase the Northern Sea Route’s annual transit capacity to between 127 million and 463 million tonnes by 2050. articles.body: Chinese ship-owner CMES holds vessel-naming ceremony in South Korea, advancing the two countries’ shipbuilding cooperation in Shipbuilding News 02/11/2026 The first vessel under China Merchants Energy Shipping’s (CMES) second-phase LNG project with QatarEnergy was named in South Korea on October 28-29, according to media reports, marking progress in cooperation between Chinese ship-owners and South Korean shipbuilders. The LEKHRAIB, the first of six 174,000-cubic-meter LNG carriers ordered by CMES from South Korea’s Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI), was named during ceremonies held on Geoje Island and in Busan. The vessel will provide long-term LNG transportation services for QatarEnergy. The project forms part of QatarEnergy’s fleet expansion to support rising LNG production and exports. In addition to the six vessels built by Samsung Heavy Industries, CMES secured long-term transportation contracts for four larger 271,000-cubic-meter QC MAX carriers, which are being built by China’s Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding. LNG carriers are among the most technologically demanding commercial vessels, as they transport natural gas at temperatures of around minus 162 C. Their construction requires specialized cargo containment and insulation systems. The LEKHRAIB features a GTT Mark III Flex membrane containment system, with a designed daily boil-off rate of no more than 0.085 percent, as well as dual-fuel engines. The project reflects the changing dynamics of the global LNG carrier market. South Korean shipbuilders have long held a strong position in large LNG carrier construction, while Chinese shipyards have been expanding their capabilities and securing more orders for advanced vessels, Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times. The participation of Samsung Heavy Industries and Hudong-Zhonghua in the same project highlights both countries’ roles in meeting growing global demand for LNG transportation. Cooperation between Chinese ship-owners and South Korean shipyards is developing alongside competition between the two countries’ shipbuilding industries, particularly in the high-end vessel market, Wang said. articles.body: South Korea’s Top Shipbuilders Post Strong Q3 Profits Amid Challenges in Shipbuilding News 02/11/2026 Amid adverse factors such as exchange rate declines, reduced working days, and labor-management conflicts, South Korea’s three major shipbuilders achieved relatively robust performance in the third quarter of this year. Samsung Heavy Industries announced on the 29th that its operating profit for the quarter increased by 42% compared to the same period last year. Combined, the operating profits of the three shipbuilders—HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering and Hanwha Ocean—totaled 2.2713 trillion Korean won. This is attributed to continued revenue from high-value-added vessels, such as liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers, which were contracted at higher prices in the past, partially offsetting cost burdens. Samsung Heavy Industries reported third-quarter revenue of 3.1504 trillion Korean won and operating profit of 338.4 billion Korean won, marking year-on-year increases of 19.6% and 42.1%, respectively. Although revenue decreased by 2.5% from the previous quarter due to reduced working days caused by summer vacations and the Chuseok holiday, operating profit rose by 4.1%. The operating margin reached 10.7%. Cumulative operating profit for the first three quarters of the year stood at 936.5 billion Korean won. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering, which disclosed its results on the 28th, saw its third-quarter operating profit surge by 37.3% year-on-year to 1.4472 trillion Korean won. Its cumulative operating profit for the year reached 4.4483 trillion Korean won, surpassing the record annual operating profit of 3.9045 trillion Korean won set last year within just three quarters. Hanwha Ocean also reported on the 27th that its third-quarter operating profit increased by 67.6% year-on-year to 485.7 billion Korean won. However, cost pressures persist in the shipbuilding industry. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering faced a 70 billion Korean won reduction in operating profit due to exchange rate declines and a 50 billion Korean won decrease from reduced working days in the third quarter. Additional costs from wage and collective bargaining (labor-management agreement) negotiations were also reflected in its results. Consequently, the company’s operating profit fell by approximately 12% from the previous quarter. Samsung Heavy Industries similarly saw revenue decline quarter-on-quarter due to reduced working days. Labor-management conflicts have largely entered the final stages of resolution. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries’ labor and management reached a final agreement on wage and collective bargaining on October 27 after 11 partial strikes and a high-altitude protest. Hanwha Ocean’s labor and management also provisionally agreed on a base pay increase of 140,000 Korean won after 30 rounds of negotiations on the same day. Samsung Heavy Industries concluded its wage negotiations last month. Source: The Chosun Daily 2026-11-02 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

Tonic South Korea’s LS Cable & System and its subsidiary, LS Marine Solution, have signed a capacity reservation agreement with Taean Wind Power for subsea cable supply and installation work on the 504MW Taean offshore wind project. The two companies are currently carrying out engineering and preliminary surveys to determine cable specifications and the final offshore installation scope. articles.body: Asia Break Bulk Expands Fleet with Four Heavy-Lift Vessel Newbuilds Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 ABB HL500 vessel rendering (Credit: ABB) Singapore-based Asia Break Bulk (ABB), part of Hamburg-based COLI Group, has signed long-term agreements with Schoeller Holdings for four new multipurpose heavy-lift vessels, with the first scheduled for delivery in October 2028. The four 12,600-DWT Octopus-type vessels, designed by CSSC-SDARI, will each feature two 250-tonne cranes capable of tandem lifts of up to 500 tonnes, expanding ABB's project cargo transportation capabilities. Each vessel will have a single box-shaped cargo hold measuring more than 89 meters in length, alongside a bridge-forward layout providing additional deck space for oversized cargo. The vessels will also feature ice class 1A, allowing winter operations in ice-affected areas, and a design optimized for fuel efficiency at a service speed of 15 knots. The first newbuild is scheduled for delivery in October 2028, with the remaining three sister vessels to follow. The fleet expansion is aimed at meeting demand for transporting heavy, oversized and complex cargoes directly to destinations with limited port infrastructure and draft restrictions, reducing the need for intermediate cargo handling. “We are seeing increasing demand from our customers for shorter transit times and direct access to ports and destinations with draft and infrastructure limitations,” said Maximilian Fischer, General Manager at Asia Break Bulk. Schoeller Holdings is partnering with ABB on the project, providing fleet development and financing expertise, while Columbia Shipmanagement will supervise the newbuilding program. articles.title: NAVTOR Upgrades NavFleet with Live AIS Vessel Monitoring
articles.summary: Maritime technology company NAVTOR has introduced real-time AIS streaming to its NavFleet platform, allowing fleet managers to monitor vessel positions, movements and surrounding traffic with minimal latency.The new capability, included in NavFleet version 2.7.1…
articles.body: NAVTOR Upgrades NavFleet with Live AIS Vessel Monitoring Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 2, 2026 NavFleet 2.7.1 - users now have the ability to zoom in on any vessel, anywhere, delivering new levels of operational insight and awareness (Credit: NAVTOR) Maritime technology company NAVTOR has introduced real-time AIS streaming to its NavFleet platform, allowing fleet managers to monitor vessel positions, movements and surrounding traffic with minimal latency. The new capability, included in NavFleet version 2.7.1, uses NAVTOR's existing digital infrastructure to capture and transmit live vessel AIS data, providing ship operators with more immediate access to information on vessel speed, heading and position. The system uses NavBox, NAVTOR's secure gateway for exchanging data between vessels and shore-based systems, to capture, package and transmit AIS information through a proprietary, low-bandwidth network. According to NAVTOR, the technology allows fleet managers to monitor vessels in the context of surrounding traffic and marine infrastructure, reducing reliance on position updates that may be several minutes or hours old. “This creates a new level of awareness for fleet managers, enabling not just better, more informed decision-making, but proactive decision-making,” said Tor Håkon Svanes, NAVTOR's NavFleet Platform Manager. The system also enables users to view vessels according to their dimensions and current operational situation, supporting monitoring and assistance during emergencies. NAVTOR said the capability provides access to vessel information without the individual vessel charges associated with some providers of high-frequency satellite AIS data. The NavFleet 2.7.1 update also introduces additional map layers, including IMMA, WCZ, PCA and IMO SA, alongside improved file sharing and further refinements to coordination between ship- and shore-based teams. NAVTOR plans to introduce AIS stream replay functionality in a future release, allowing users to review historical vessel movements alongside associated contextual information. The proposed feature could be used to examine incidents involving vessels and port infrastructure by reviewing information such as a ship's approach angle, speed and wind direction. NavFleet 2.7.1 is available as an automatic upgrade for existing NavFleet monitoring subscribers, while AIS streaming will become available through the NavFleet App in December 2026.

November 2, 2026 © Miha Creative / Adobe Stock Oil fell nearly 4% on Monday as talks between Iranian and Qatari officials on a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran raised hopes that Middle East supply disruptions could ease. Iranian negotiators left Doha talks on Sunday, but not due to difficulties in negotiations, an official briefed on the meeting told Reuters on Monday. "The new month brought with it renewed hopes of a breakthrough in the Iranian stalemate," said Tamas Varga of oil broker PVM. Brent crude futures LCOc1 fell $4.20, or 3.7%, to $109.23 a barrel by 0900 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude CLc1 traded at $100.14, down $3.98, or 3.8%. Brent ended October at its highest in six months amid concerns that the US-Iran conflict could escalate again after Tuesday's US midterm elections. "Lingering hopes of some form of diplomatic progress, combined with the absence of any meaningful military escalation over the weekend, have taken some of the immediate heat out of prices for now," said Tim Waterer, chief ⁠market analyst at KCM Trade. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the purpose of the "ongoing and progressing" talks was to continue consultations with the Qatari mediators, adding Tehran was prepared for "both defence and diplomacy". The talks follow a recent increase in attacks on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, although there are also signs of shipments rising from some major exporters. In October, Saudi Arabia increased crude exports versus September despite attacks by the Iran-aligned Yemeni Houthis on its energy infrastructure, two of three ship-tracking companies said. The outbreak of the Iran war at the end of February has depleted oil stocks. The world has drained nearly 1 billion oil barrels from inventories since the war disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the CEO of Abu Dhabi's state-owned oil company ADNOC said. Oil could still rise further, some analysts say. Goldman Sachs raised its oil price forecasts on Sunday due to elevated supply risks and said Brent could jump to $140 in 2027 if Gulf oil output stays 3.5 million barrels per day below its 2025 average. "Intensified shipping attacks, damage to oil infrastructure, and a more persistent risk premium remain the key triggers of potential upside," the bank said in a report. articles.body: CMA CGM has announced a new War Risk Surcharge (WRS) for shipments to and from Black Sea countries. The carrier has also updated its Dangerous Goods Surcharge for selected routes connecting Europe, North Africa and the Red Sea. The measures introduce a US$35 per TEU war risk charge for Black Sea shipments and a US$150 per TEU charge for specified dangerous goods movements. War risk surcharge for Black Sea shipments CMA CGM will introduce a War Risk Surcharge of US$35 per TEU on all cargo moving to and from Black Sea countries, effective 9 November 2026. However, the surcharge will take effect on 1 December 2026 for the United States and its territories, Australia, New Zealand and Latin American countries subject to regulatory filing requirements. According to the carrier, the operational situation in the Black Sea has deteriorated over recent months. The company also cited the Joint War Committee’s designation of the Black Sea maritime area as a war risk zone on 16 September 2026. As a result, voyages in the region face additional costs, prompting CMA CGM to introduce the surcharge to maintain service continuity. The carrier stated that it continues to monitor conditions in the region and will provide customers with voyage-specific information when required. Dangerous goods surcharge updated for Red Sea routes Meanwhile, CMA CGM has announced an updated Dangerous Goods Surcharge of US$150 per TEU for selected shipments originating in North Europe, the Mediterranean and North Africa. The charge applies to all cargo classified under the International Maritime Dangerous Goods (IMDG) Code moving to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia and Port Sudan in Sudan. In addition, the same surcharge applies to IMDG shipments from these origin regions to the Indian Subcontinent via Jeddah. Both dangerous goods surcharge provisions took effect on 27 October 2026. The announced charges are separate from other applicable freight costs. These may include bunker-related surcharges, terminal handling charges, security fees and other local charges.

Mortier takes over from Petraki, who was first elected president in October 2022 and served two consecutive terms. WISTA has strengthened its international standing during that period, building on its consultative status with the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and expanding initiatives aimed at increasing women’s representation in shipping. Serica Energy has signed a contract for the Odfjell Drilling-operated Beacon Pacific rig to execute a multi-well UKCS drilling campaign, targeting high-return, near-field opportunities across the North Sea operator's portfolio, with the potential to add up to 30,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boepd) of incremental production, helping to sustain portfolio production of 50,000 boepd into the next decade. The contract encompasses a firm scope of six wells, along with further options for additional activity. Drilling is expected to begin in Q3 2027 with the first wells drilled at the Bruce field since 2012, targeting more than 10,000 boepd of incremental production, with the potential for first production approximately 12 months from the start of drilling activities. " Securing the rig is an important milestone in delivering our organic growth program. Utilizing the Beacon Pacific also gives us the operational flexibility to progress additional opportunities across Kyla and the Greater Laggan Area, following partner and regulatory approval, maintaining momentum in our wider UKCS portfolio. articles.title: StormGeo acquires Portchain to expand voyage optimization capabilities
articles.summary: StormGeo, part of Alfa Laval, has acquired Danish maritime technology company Portchain, expanding its capabilities in voyage optimization and port call coordination. The acquisition was completed on 30 October 2026 and brings Portchain’s container terminal coordination technology into StormGeo’s maritime digital...
articles.body: StormGeo, part of Alfa Laval, has acquired Danish maritime technology company Portchain, expanding its capabilities in voyage optimization and port call coordination. The acquisition was completed on 30 October 2026 and brings Portchain’s container terminal coordination technology into StormGeo’s maritime digital solutions portfolio. The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the transaction. Portchain connects container shipping lines and terminals through shared operational data. Its network currently includes more than 200 terminals, representing over 40% of global container terminal capacity, according to the company. Connecting voyage planning with port operations The acquisition aims to bring voyage optimization and berth planning closer together, allowing shipping companies to make more informed operational decisions. StormGeo’s Voyage Intelligence platform supports route planning, vessel performance monitoring and fuel consumption optimization. Meanwhile, Portchain provides real-time information on vessel schedules, berth availability and terminal operations. Its Portchain Connect platform supports coordination between carriers and terminals, while Portchain Quay helps terminals manage berth allocation, cranes and workforce planning. By combining these capabilities, the companies aim to improve Just-in-Time vessel arrivals. For example, changes in berth availability could allow operators to adjust vessel speeds while ships are still at sea. This approach could help reduce unnecessary waiting times, fuel consumption and emissions. It could also improve arrival predictability and support terminal resource planning. Kim Hedegaard Sørensen, Business Unit President at StormGeo, said the acquisition would help connect weather intelligence and voyage planning with updated information from ports and terminals. Meanwhile, Niels Kristiansen, CEO of Portchain, highlighted the opportunity to bring voyage optimization and port call coordination closer together through StormGeo’s international network. The acquisition follows the continued expansion of Portchain’s terminal network, including the addition of the Port of Drammen to Portchain Connect , previously reported by Container News. Portchain will continue operating as an independent company under StormGeo for the next few years. It will subsequently be integrated into StormGeo’s portfolio. According to the companies, existing Portchain customers will experience no service disruption during the transition.

The acquisition was completed on 30 October 2026 and brings Portchain’s container terminal coordination technology into StormGeo’s maritime digital solutions portfolio.

articles.body: Production & Processing November 2, 2026 · 1 minute ago Subsea7 wins EPCI contract for fast-track oil development off Norway NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Subsea7 Subsea7 has secured an engineering, procurement, construction and installation (EPCI) contract with Aker BP for the fast-track Lyra field development project, previously known as Kjøttkake, offshore Norway. Located in the northern part of the North Sea, approximately 44 kilometers from the Gjøa platform, the Lyra field development will be tied back to the existing Gjøa platform through the NOVA field infrastructure. Subsea7's scope includes EPCI of gas lift and production pipelines and associated subsea infrastructure. According to the company, the production pipeline will feature a pipe-in-pipe design and offshore installation activities will be executed using vessels from its fleet. Project management and engineering activities will begin immediately at Subsea7's office in Stavanger, Norway, while pipeline fabrication will take place at the spool base at Vigra, Norway. Offshore operations are scheduled for execution during 2026, 2027 and 2028. Subsea7 said the contract was substantial, which it defines as being between $150 million and $300 million. "Lyra showcases the strength of the Aker BP Subsea Alliance. From securing long-lead items to mobilising engineering, fabrication and offshore resources, this award demonstrates Subsea7’s ability to deliver first production at exceptional speed," said Erik Femsteinevik , Vice President Norway at Subsea7. "We are excited to support Aker BP on another landmark development and proud to bring the expertise of our Stavanger and Vigra teams to a project that will deliver significant value for our client, partners and the Norwegian Continental Shelf." articles.title: ZIM launches new ZX3 express service connecting China and Los Angeles
articles.summary: ZIM Integrated Shipping Services has announced the launch of ZX3, a new premium express container service connecting Shanghai and Xiamen in China with Los Angeles on the US West Coast. The new service is scheduled to begin operations in December 2026 and will operate exclusively under ZIM. It will offer a direct...
articles.body: ZIM Integrated Shipping Services has announced the launch of ZX3, a new premium express container service connecting Shanghai and Xiamen in China with Los Angeles on the US West Coast. The new service is scheduled to begin operations in December 2026 and will operate exclusively under ZIM. It will offer a direct transit time of 12 days from Shanghai to Los Angeles and 15 days from Xiamen. New ZX3 service expands ZIM’s transpacific network The new ZX3 service will follow the port rotation: Xiamen – Shanghai – Los Angeles – Xiamen ZX3 will join ZIM’s existing premium express services, ZEX and ZX2. Together, the three services will provide seven weekly departures from China and Vietnam to the US West Coast. At the Port of Los Angeles, ZX3 will call at the West Basin Container Terminal (WBCT). According to ZIM, the service will benefit from a dedicated berth, container yard and pickup lanes. In addition, the carrier plans Monday arrivals in Los Angeles, with expedited cargo availability. Containers will be discharged onto dedicated chassis, allowing immediate pickup without appointments or queues. The service will also offer rail connections to major inland destinations across the United States. These include Chicago, New York, Memphis, Dallas and Kansas City. Hani Kalinski, Executive Vice President of ZIM’s Pacific Business Unit, said the new service will expand the company’s premium network coverage and provide additional flexibility for customers. The launch strengthens ZIM’s expedited transpacific offering by introducing a dedicated premium connection from Xiamen and an additional direct service from Shanghai to Los Angeles.

MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Prospector 5 jack-up rig Source: Borr Drilling As search and rescue operations continue in the waters off Gabon, one worker remains unaccounted for following the sinking of a 2014-built jack-up rig. Bermuda-headquartered offshore drilling contractor Borr Drilling has disclosed the start of an independent probe to establish the circumstances that led to the tragic incident. In an update on the Prospector 5 incident in Gabonese waters, Borr Drilling confirmed that the body of a fourth individual was located, with one more offshore worker still missing after the 2014-built jack-up experienced a punch-through event at approximately 20:37 local time on October 24, 2026, during preload activities, which led to loss of stability and the subsequent sinking of the rig with 115 personnel on board. The Marshall Islands-flagged vessel was sailing toward the waterway loaded with LNG from Qatar when it came under fire, the people said, asking not to be named as they are not authorized to speak to the media. Just hours earlier, Iranian authorities were understood to have provided a green light, they added. The ship subsequently turned around and headed into the Persian Gulf, according to ship-tracking data. “Qatar reserves its right to take all necessary measures, in accordance with international law and the UN Charter, to protect its assets and safeguard its vessels and their crews,” the Qatari Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Sunday, adding that authorities are investigating the incident and those responsible. He said all 25 crew members, including six Indian nationals, were safe but didn’t provide further details. Qatar Gas Transport Company Ltd., known as Nakilat, said on Sunday that the carrier remained operational and was being assessed. It wasn’t immediately clear why the tanker came under fire or whether it would still attempt to reach its destination. Pakistan , apparently benefiting from its ties with Iran and its role as mediator, has communicated with Iranian authorities over the safety of several other shipments of Qatari LNG over the past month, all of which crossed successfully into the Gulf of Oman. The incident underscores the continued risk for vessels navigating around Hormuz and poses a fresh challenge for Pakistan, which has grappled for months with an energy shortfall as a result of upheaval in the Middle East. Without the LNG shipment, Pakistan could be forced to turn to the spot market, where prices are more than three times pre-war levels.
